parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A teacher phones a youth hostel to book a school trip.
script: Good morning, Valley View Youth Hostel, Greg speaking.
Hello. I'm a teacher, and I'd like to book accommodation for a school trip.
Of course. Could I have your name?
It's Clare Fenwick. F, E, N, W, I, C, K.
And the name of the school?
How many students will there be?
We were expecting thirty, but some can't come, so it's twenty-four now.
When would you like to arrive?
On Wednesday the twelfth of May, for three nights.
That's fine. The students would be in dormitories of six beds each, and the teachers have their own rooms.
Breakfast and dinner are served in the dining room, and on days when you're out walking, we can provide packed lunches.
Great. Do you organise any activities?
We have a guided walk to the waterfall, which is very popular with school groups. Shall I book that for you?
Yes, please. And what's the cost?
It's twenty-eight pounds per student per night, including all meals.
Teachers stay free, as long as there's one teacher for every ten students.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A radio presenter gives information about road closures for a city marathon.
script: Good morning. This is Neil Barker with travel news. As many of you know, the city marathon takes place this Sunday, and this year, for the first time, the route goes through the historic city centre.
Around twelve thousand runners are expected, a big increase on last year's eight thousand, so there'll be a lot of disruption.
Buses will still run, but they'll be diverted away from the centre until about three in the afternoon. Please check the bus company's website for details.
If you live on the route, you're advised to move your car off the street before Saturday night, as any vehicles left on the route will be towed away.
Now, the road closures. Bridge Street will be closed all day, as it's where the start and finish areas are being set up.
Park Road will be closed from six until ten in the morning, while the faster runners pass through.
The High Street will be closed from seven in the morning until two in the afternoon.
Station Road, I'm pleased to say, will remain open as normal, so you'll still be able to reach the railway station.
Queen's Avenue is also closed from seven a.m. until two p.m.
And finally, Mill Lane will be closed from six until ten in the morning.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two engineering students, Jess and Kwame, discuss their solar boat project.
script: Jess, have you read the competition rules for the solar boat race?
Yes. Most of them are fine, but the weight limit is going to be our biggest problem. The whole boat can't weigh more than forty kilograms.
That's why I wanted to use carbon fibre for the hull.
It's light, but it's far too expensive for our budget. I think plywood is the best option. It's cheap and quite light if we use thin sheets.
OK, plywood then. What about the solar panels? Should we angle them towards the sun?
It would generate a bit more power, but they'd catch the wind and make the boat unstable. I'd lay them flat on the deck.
Fair enough. My main worry is the batteries. Last year, another team's batteries overheated in the race.
We'll need to make sure there's enough air around them. When can we test the boat?
The university lake is free next Saturday. Let's do it then.
Good. Now, let's divide the tasks. I'll design the hull, since I've done the drawings already.
And I'll do the wiring for the motor.
We should both write the report, because the judges give a lot of marks for it.
Agreed. Who's going to contact sponsors?
I will. My uncle works for a solar energy company, so I'll start with him.
Then I'll build the trailer to transport the boat.

parts.title: Part 4
script: Today's lecture is about the emperor penguin, the largest penguin species and one of the toughest animals on the planet.
Emperor penguins are the only animals that breed during the Antarctic winter, when temperatures can fall as low as minus sixty degrees Celsius and winds reach two hundred kilometres an hour.
After the female lays a single egg, she passes it carefully to the male and then walks back to the sea to feed, sometimes travelling more than a hundred kilometres across the ice.

The male keeps the egg warm by balancing it on his feet, under a fold of skin. For about one hundred and fifteen days, from the time they arrive at the breeding site, the males eat nothing at all, surviving on their fat reserves.

To survive the cold, the males huddle together in groups of thousands. The birds constantly shuffle, taking turns at the edge of the huddle, where it's coldest, so that no individual stays exposed for too long.
Emperors are also remarkable divers. They can dive to depths of around five hundred metres and stay underwater for more than twenty minutes while hunting fish and squid.

But they face a serious threat. Emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice, which must last from April until December, when the chicks have grown waterproof feathers. In 2022, the sea ice in parts of Antarctica broke up early, and several colonies lost almost all their chicks, which drowned or froze.
Scientists warn that, if current warming continues, emperor penguins could be close to extinction by 2100.

passages.title: Folding Into the Future
paragraphs: Although paper was invented in China, the art of paper folding, or origami, is most closely associated with Japan, where it has been practised for centuries. For a long time, designs were passed on by demonstration and memory. This changed in the twentieth century thanks to Akira Yoshizawa, who created thousands of original models and developed a system of symbols, such as dotted lines and arrows, to show how to fold them. His system is still used in origami books around the world.

In recent decades, origami has attracted the interest of mathematicians and engineers. One of the most influential is Robert Lang, who worked as a physicist at NASA before becoming a full-time origami artist. Lang showed that the folding patterns needed to create complex shapes could be calculated mathematically, and he developed computer programs that design origami models automatically.

One of the most famous examples of origami in engineering is the Miura fold, invented by the Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura. It is a pattern of folds that allows a large flat sheet to be folded into a compact block and then opened in a single movement, simply by pulling on two opposite corners. Miura developed it as a way of packing large structures for space. In 1995, it was used for a folded solar array on a Japanese satellite, which unfolded once the satellite was in orbit.

The same challenge, how to fit something huge into a small rocket, faced the designers of the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021. Its main mirror, made of 18 hexagonal segments, was too large to fit inside the rocket and had to be folded. So did its sunshield, which is roughly the size of a tennis court when fully opened. The unfolding process, carried out far from Earth, involved hundreds of steps, each of which had to work perfectly.

Origami ideas are also being applied in medicine. Researchers at the University of Oxford have designed stents, small tubes used to hold open blood vessels, that can be folded into a tiny shape, inserted into the body and then opened in the right place. Such designs are still being tested and are not yet in general use. Car manufacturers, meanwhile, have used origami mathematics to work out how to fold airbags so that they open quickly and safely.

Perhaps the most futuristic application is in robotics. Engineers have built flat robots that can fold themselves into three-dimensional shapes and then walk away. The ancient art of folding paper, it seems, may help to shape some of the technologies of the future.

passages.title: Disappearing Ice
paragraphs: Glaciers are among the most important sources of fresh water on Earth. Mountain glaciers in particular act as natural 'water towers', storing snowfall in winter and releasing it gradually as meltwater in the warmer months. The glaciers of the Himalayas and nearby mountain ranges feed rivers on which nearly two billion people depend for drinking water, farming and electricity.

Almost everywhere, these glaciers are shrinking. A major international study published in 2025, which combined many different measurement methods, estimated that the world's glaciers, excluding the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, lost around 270 billion tonnes of ice per year between 2000 and 2023. The rate of loss was considerably higher in the second half of that period than in the first.

In the short term, melting glaciers can actually increase the amount of water flowing in rivers. But this cannot last. Scientists use the term 'peak water' to describe the point at which meltwater reaches its maximum and then begins to decline as the glacier gets smaller. Many glaciers in the Andes and the Alps are thought to have already passed this point, and some Himalayan rivers are expected to reach it within the next few decades.

Melting glaciers also create new dangers. As ice retreats, meltwater often collects in lakes held back by natural dams of rock and ice. If such a dam suddenly fails, perhaps because of an earthquake or a landslide into the lake, the water can rush down the valley as a glacial lake outburst flood. In 2023, a flood of this kind in the Indian state of Sikkim destroyed a hydroelectric dam and killed dozens of people.

Some glaciers have already disappeared completely. In 2014, Iceland's Okjökull glacier was officially declared to have lost its status as a glacier, because it no longer had enough ice to move under its own weight. In 2019, scientists and local people placed a memorial plaque at the site, addressed to future generations.

Communities have begun to respond in creative ways. In the dry Himalayan region of Ladakh, the engineer Sonam Wangchuk developed 'ice stupas', tall cones of ice built in winter by spraying water into the freezing air. They melt slowly in spring, providing water for crops at the time farmers need it most. In Switzerland, parts of the Rhône Glacier are covered each summer with white blankets to reflect sunlight and slow melting. Such measures can help locally, but scientists stress that they cannot replace large cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.

passages.title: The Trouble With Open-Plan Offices
paragraphs: Walk into almost any modern office and you are likely to see rows of desks in a large open space, with few walls or doors. The open-plan office has become the standard design for companies around the world, promoted as a way to encourage communication, creativity and teamwork. Yet the evidence suggests that it often achieves the opposite.

The idea has a long history. In the 1950s, German consultants developed the 'Bürolandschaft', or office landscape, in which desks were arranged in irregular groups according to how information flowed between workers, rather than in strict rows. In the 1960s, the American designer Robert Propst created the 'Action Office', a flexible system of movable panels intended to give workers more freedom and variety. Ironically, companies turned his ideas into the cramped grey cubicle, which Propst himself later criticised.

The modern open office, inspired partly by technology companies, removed the cubicle walls altogether. The results have been disappointing. In a study published in 2018, researchers at Harvard tracked employees at two companies before and after they moved from cubicles to open-plan offices. Face-to-face interaction fell by around 70 percent, while the use of email and instant messaging increased. When people know that everyone can see and hear them, it seems, they become more reluctant to start conversations.

Noise is the most common complaint. Overheard conversations are particularly distracting, because the brain automatically tries to follow speech. Many employees respond by wearing headphones, creating a kind of private space in the middle of a shared room, but this also signals to colleagues that they do not wish to be disturbed, which further reduces communication.

Why, then, have open-plan offices become so widespread? In my view, the main reason is not collaboration but cost. Open offices allow companies to fit far more workers into the same space, and 'hot-desking', in which employees have no fixed desk, reduces the amount of space needed even further. These savings are real and easy to measure, while the losses in concentration and wellbeing are harder to calculate.

None of this means that every worker needs a private office, which would be expensive and could isolate staff. A more promising approach is 'activity-based working', in which offices provide different spaces for different kinds of work: quiet rooms for focused tasks, open areas for teamwork and small rooms for private calls. I believe that offering a mixture of spaces, and allowing employees to choose between them, is the best way to meet the needs of both organisations and the people who work in them.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the percentage of household income spent on five categories in one country in 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the proportion of household income spent on housing, food, transport, entertainment and clothing in one country in 1990 and 2020.

Overall, housing was the largest area of spending in both years, and its share increased considerably. In contrast, the proportion spent on food and clothing fell, while spending on transport and entertainment rose slightly.
In 1990, households spent a quarter of their income on housing and almost as much, 22%, on food. Transport accounted for 12%, clothing for 9% and entertainment for just 6%.

By 2020, the share spent on housing had risen by ten percentage points to 35%, more than double the share for any other category. Food spending, by contrast, fell sharply to 14%, the same level as transport, which had increased slightly. The proportion spent on entertainment rose to 9%, overtaking clothing, whose share almost halved to 5%.

task2.text: Some people think that famous people, such as sports stars and celebrities, have a responsibility to be good role models for young people. Others believe that their private lives are their own business. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Celebrities and sports stars are followed by millions of young people, especially on social media. This has led to debate about whether they have a duty to behave as role models. While I accept that famous people are entitled to some privacy, I believe that they do have a responsibility to behave reasonably in public.

Those who argue that celebrities' private lives are their own business make several valid points. Famous people did not choose to become role models; a footballer is paid for playing football, not for setting a moral example. Like everyone else, they make mistakes, and constant media attention can make ordinary errors seem like scandals. Moreover, it could be argued that parents, teachers and communities, rather than strangers on television, should be the main influences on children's values.

However, I find the opposite view more persuasive. Young people often copy the behaviour, language and attitudes of the people they admire, whether this is positive or negative. When a famous athlete speaks out against racism or supports a charity, many young fans follow their example. In the same way, celebrities who promote unhealthy products, glorify violence or behave aggressively can have a harmful influence. Because their fame brings enormous financial rewards, it seems reasonable to expect a degree of responsibility in return.

That said, this responsibility should be limited to public behaviour. Celebrities should be held accountable for what they say and do in public and online, but their private relationships and family lives should be respected.
In conclusion, although famous people deserve some privacy, I believe their influence on young people means they should try to set a positive example in their public behaviour.

speaking.cue:
Describe a person you know who is successful.
You should say:
- who this person is
- what they have achieved
- how they became successful
and explain what you have learned from them.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about my aunt, who runs her own small business making and selling handmade bags. She's my mother's younger sister, and I've watched her business grow over the past ten years. She started with almost nothing. After she lost her job at a garment factory, she began sewing bags at home from leftover fabric and selling them to neighbours. Then a friend suggested she put some photos online, and that changed everything. Now she has a small workshop, employs six women from her area, and sells her bags across the country through social media, and even to a few customers abroad. What I admire most is how she did it. She didn't have a business degree or any money to invest, but she was incredibly persistent and willing to learn. She taught herself photography, how to manage orders, and how to deal with difficult customers, mostly by watching videos at night after a full day of work. She also made a lot of mistakes, like the time she ordered far too much fabric, but she never gave up. The main thing I've learned from her is that success doesn't depend on having the perfect start. It depends on being willing to try, learn from failures and keep going.
